question: Why is recording past medical and surgical history important during an admission assessment?

options.A: It replaces the need to ask about current medications
options.B: It predicts the exact date the patient will be discharged
options.C: It proves the patient has visited a hospital before
options.D: It helps identify chronic conditions that may affect current treatment

explanation: Knowing past health problems helps the healthcare team anticipate complications and tailor current therapy safely. [learn more](GNS123_U2_T2#GNS123_U2_T2_h3)

question: Which of the following is a primary reason why women with FGM experience higher rates of birth asphyxia for their infants?

options.A: Anesthetic drugs cross the placenta and paralyze the fetus.
options.B: The placenta detaches prematurely due to maternal pelvic pain.
options.C: Umbilical cord blood flow stops during the first trimester.
options.D: Rigid scar tissue delays the descent of the baby through the birth canal.

explanation: Inflexible scar tissue obstructs labor progress, prolonging the delivery process and depriving the newborn of adequate oxygen. [learn more](GNS312_U1_T6#GNS312_U1_T6_h4)

question: Why is continuous heart monitoring a must right after a successful defibrillation?

options.A: To ensure the patient stays awake during recovery
options.B: To verify that the defibrillator battery is still fully charged
options.C: To measure the exact electrical resistance of the skin
options.D: To catch early warning signs of recurrent arrhythmias or re-arrest

explanation: Just because the heart restarted doesn't mean they're out of the woods. These patients are very fragile and can easily slip right back into a dangerous rhythm.

question: Why do we use air ambulances for patients in remote areas?

options.A: It bridges the gap to advanced medical facilities
options.B: It is always cheaper than ground ambulance transport
options.C: Patients prefer flying over riding in cars
options.D: Hospitals do not accept ground transfers

explanation: Spot on! When patients are far away from big hospitals, air transport moves them quickly so they can get the high-level care they desperately need.

question: How does provider bias negatively affect women seeking post-abortion care?

options.A: It automatically lowers the cost of prescription antibiotics and painkillers
options.B: It causes delays in treatment, poor quality care, and discourages women from seeking help
options.C: It improves the speed at which emergency surgical instruments are sterilized
options.D: It guarantees that the patient receives specialized psychological therapy

explanation: Spot on. When health workers show judgmental attitudes, patients hide information or avoid health facilities, making things worse.

question: In a strongly patriarchal setting, who usually makes the final decision on family size?

options.A: The junior nursing officer
options.B: The male head of the household
options.C: The youngest child in the family
options.D: The local government chairman

explanation: Correct! In these settings, men or senior family members traditionally call the shots on major household matters like family size.

question: Which client should you, as a nurse, keep a close eye on for signs of complicated grief?

options.A: A client who cries openly while talking about a loved one during the first week after a death
options.B: A client who expresses persistent bitterness and an inability to accept a sudden loss many months later
options.C: A client who finds comfort in sharing memories of the deceased with close friends
options.D: A client who participates in traditional funeral and memorial services

explanation: Spot on! Holding onto deep bitterness and refusing to accept the reality months down the track are red flags for complicated grief.

question: A patient comes in with fever, right upper tummy pain, dark urine, and yellow eyes a few weeks after getting injections at an unlicensed clinic. What is the most likely condition?

options.A: Acute viral hepatitis
options.B: Iron deficiency anemia
options.C: Chronic kidney disease
options.D: Acute bacterial sepsis

explanation: Dark urine and yellow eyes (jaundice) are classic signs of liver trouble like acute viral hepatitis, often linked to unsafe injection exposures.

question: What is the medical word for excessively heavy or long menstrual periods?

options.A: Menorrhagia
options.B: Amenorrhea
options.C: Dysmenorrhea
options.D: Menarche

explanation: You can remember this easily: 'Menorrhagia' means very heavy monthly flow that gets in the way of a woman's daily life and comfort.

question: What is the primary role of the nurse within the multidisciplinary palliative care team?

options.A: Making all final medical diagnoses and prescribing drugs alone
options.B: Replacing the family members during visiting hours
options.C: Acting as a central hub of communication and coordinating care
options.D: Handling the financial billing and insurance claims for the hospital

explanation: Nurses spend the most time at the bedside, making them uniquely positioned to coordinate input from all team members. [learn more](GNS321_U4_T15#GNS321_U4_T15_h8)

question: A patient has a painful surgical wound oozing foul-smelling yellow fluid. What test should the nurse expect the doctor to order first?

options.A: Arterial blood gas analysis
options.B: Chest X-ray examination
options.C: Complete metabolic panel
options.D: Wound culture and sensitivity

explanation: Correct! A wound culture lets the lab identify the exact troublemaker germ and figure out which antibiotic will wipe it out best.

question: What happens in the body during the resistance stage of stress?

options.A: The sympathetic nervous system shuts down completely
options.B: Energy reserves are fully depleted and the person collapses
options.C: The body attempts to adapt and cope with the ongoing stressor
options.D: No hormonal or physiological changes take place

explanation: During resistance, your body tries its best to balance things out and keep functioning despite the ongoing pressure. It's like your internal battery working overtime to keep you going!

question: Which of these details must you include when charting steam tent therapy?

options.A: The brand name of the plastic tent canopy
options.B: The exact electrical voltage of the wall socket
options.C: The name of the manufacturer who built the bed
options.D: Start and end times of the treatment

explanation: You got it! Accurate start and end times give a clear timeline of the care you provided.

question: Why should a nurse avoid documenting subjective opinions like 'patient is lying about how she got these bruises' in a clinical chart?

options.A: Because patients are not allowed to read their own medical folders
options.B: Because clinical records require objective facts and direct quotes for legal validity
options.C: Because personal opinions are always illegal to write down
options.D: Because hospital management does not read nursing notes

explanation: Accurate, unbiased documentation protects the patient's legal rights and maintains professional nursing standards. [learn more](GNS312_U4_T12#GNS312_U4_T12_h5)

question: Which condition is an MRI scan especially useful for diagnosing in the spine?

options.A: Herniated or slipped discs
options.B: Simple hairline bone fractures
options.C: Acute internal bleeding from trauma
options.D: Bacterial pneumonia infections

explanation: MRI is the best imaging choice for soft tissues of the spine, such as nerves, discs, and the spinal cord. [learn more](GNS123_U2_T12#GNS123_U2_T12_h3)

question: Why is addressing psychosocial well-being particularly important for patients with visible, chronic skin conditions?

options.A: Visible skin problems can cause embarrassment, anxiety, and social withdrawal
options.B: Emotional stress directly stops all topical medications from working
options.C: Mental health counseling replaces the need for any physical wound care
options.D: Patients with skin disorders never experience physical pain, only worry

explanation: Chronic and visible dermatological conditions frequently affect body image and self-esteem, making psychological support an important part of holistic care. [learn more](GNS213_U5_T10#GNS213_U5_T10_h8)

question: A nurse notices the clinic frequently runs out of safety boxes, causing staff to leave used needles on trays. What is the best action to take?

options.A: Ignore the issue since it does not affect direct patient treatment
options.B: Report the supply shortage to management and request immediate replenishment
options.C: Tell staff to begin washing and reusing the disposable needles instead
options.D: Instruct patients to bring their own plastic containers from home

explanation: Being a nurse advocate means speaking up when safety supplies run low so we can protect our healthcare team and our community. Great clinical leadership!

question: What do we call the body's natural ability to keep its internal environment balanced and stable?

options.A: Homeostasis
options.B: Catabolism
options.C: Anabolism
options.D: Metabolism

explanation: Homeostasis is like the body's internal thermostat—it constantly works behind the scenes to keep everything stable, no matter what is happening around you! [learn more](GNS123_U3_T15#GNS123_U3_T15_h1)

question: Which part of the eye provides the majority of its light-focusing power?

options.A: The iris
options.B: The retina
options.C: The lens
options.D: The cornea

explanation: The cornea is the clear front surface of the eye that handles most of the heavy lifting when it comes to bending and focusing incoming light. [learn more](GNS311_U3_T3#GNS311_U3_T3_h1)

question: A woman who underwent FGM as a child is admitted in active labor. What is she at higher risk for during delivery?

options.A: Rapid, painless delivery due to relaxed pelvic muscles
options.B: Obstructed labor and severe tearing from scar tissue
options.C: Complete absence of uterine contractions
options.D: Instant healing of the perineal area after birth

explanation: Scar tissue from FGM lacks elasticity, often blocking the birth canal and causing severe tearing during childbirth. [learn more](GNS312_U1_T5#GNS312_U1_T5_h3)

question: What is the main focus of client-centered drug administration?

options.A: Following hospital medication schedules without exception
options.B: Leaving medication management entirely to the doctor
options.C: Reducing the time nurses spend talking to patients
options.D: Treating the patient as an active partner in their care

explanation: Client-centered care values the patient's active participation in their own treatment plan rather than treating them as a passive recipient. [learn more](GNS125_U3_T3#GNS125_U3_T3_h1)

question: What does 'Total Fertility Rate' (TFR) actually measure?

options.A: The percentage of women using modern family planning methods
options.B: The average number of children a woman has during her reproductive years
options.C: The average age of mothers when giving birth to their first child
options.D: The total number of children born in a single hospital annually

explanation: Exactly! TFR estimates the average number of children a woman is expected to have throughout her childbearing years.

question: Which of these is NOT a common financial or social barrier to healthcare access in Nigeria?

options.A: High out-of-pocket expenses for routine medications and blood tests
options.B: Financial strain caused by the loss of daily income during hospital admissions
options.C: Free and unlimited universal healthcare coverage for all citizens
options.D: Long travel distances from rural villages to tertiary teaching hospitals

explanation: If only! Sadly, free universal healthcare isn't the reality yet, meaning out-of-pocket costs remain a huge hurdle for many patients.

question: When should a nurse hold off on starting AROM exercises?

options.A: Mild fatigue from staying in bed
options.B: A recent unstable bone fracture
options.C: A history of chronic mild backaches
options.D: Stable and well-controlled high blood pressure

explanation: Safety first! Moving a broken, unstable bone before it heals can displace it and cause serious harm.

question: Why do blood vessels swell and open up wider during inflammation?

options.A: To prevent the complement proteins from entering the injury site
options.B: To lower local tissue temperature and stop bacterial growth
options.C: To allow white blood cells and fluid to move easily into infected tissues
options.D: To slow down local blood flow so pathogens can multiply and be counted

explanation: Spot on! Opening the blood vessels lets protective white blood cells and fluid rush straight to the injury or infection site.

question: A patient arrives at the emergency unit with severe trauma. Following the ABCDE approach, what should you check first?

options.A: Skin temperature
options.B: Airway patency
options.C: Hidden body wounds
options.D: Neurological status

explanation: Always follow the alphabet! Airway comes first before anything else because getting oxygen flowing is our top priority.

question: What is the best nursing action when taking care of a patient with a bleeding disorder?

options.A: Checking core body temperature using a rectal thermometer
options.B: Applying direct pressure to venipuncture sites for an extended time
options.C: Administering all routine medications via intramuscular injection
options.D: Encouraging participation in high-contact competitive sports

explanation: Giving a little extra pressure after drawing blood or giving an injection gives that soft platelet plug enough time to form and prevents nasty bruises (hematomas)!

question: A cancer patient says food smells too strong and tastes like metal. What is a helpful nursing tip?

options.A: Suggest serving foods cool or at room temperature to reduce strong smells
options.B: Tell the patient to force themselves to eat large portions anyway
options.C: Advise the patient to stop eating completely until treatment ends
options.D: Recommend adding extra iron supplements to every meal

explanation: Warm foods release strong vapors that trigger nausea. Serving meals cool helps hide those metallic tastes and smells. Clever nursing care!

question: Why do nurses always stress taking birth control pills at the exact same time every single day?

options.A: It ensures the monthly period starts on a weekend
options.B: It reduces the financial cost of the medication pack
options.C: It maintains steady hormone levels in the bloodstream
options.D: It prevents the client from forgetting to eat meals

explanation: Consistency is key! Taking it at the same time keeps hormone levels steady so breakthrough ovulation doesn't sneak through.

question: Why do we need a whole team of different specialists (a multidisciplinary team) in neuro-rehab?

options.A: Hospital regulations require at least five different specialists to sign off on every therapy session.
options.B: It ensures that the client spends the entire day participating in continuous physical exercise.
options.C: Neurological deficits affect many different aspects of physical, cognitive, and social function.
options.D: Physicians are generally unable to manage any physical therapy exercises on their own.

explanation: Brain and nerve issues don't just affect walking—they can touch speech, thinking, emotions, and movement. That's why working together as a team gives the patient the best possible support!

question: Why might a doctor prescribe a topical NSAID gel instead of pills for sore joints?

options.A: It provides localized relief with fewer systemic side effects
options.B: It permanently restores lost joint cartilage
options.C: It cures the disease much faster than pills
options.D: It completely eliminates the need for physical therapy

explanation: Spot on! Putting medicine right on the sore joint gives great relief while protecting your stomach and kidneys from the side effects of pills.

question: Why do nurses need to understand how different imaging tests work?

options.A: To operate the heavy imaging machinery during off-peak night shifts
options.B: To independently prescribe the exact type of scan a patient needs in an emergency
options.C: To safely coordinate studies, prepare patients, and guide nursing care based on results
options.D: To replace the radiologist in reading detailed cross-sectional scans

explanation: You won't be running the big scanner machines yourself, but knowing how each test works helps you prep your patient and understand what the results mean for their care!

question: What usually triggers the body to develop secondary polycythaemia?

options.A: An autoimmune attack on bone marrow
options.B: An inherited defect in the platelets
options.C: Sudden heavy blood loss from injury
options.D: Chronic low oxygen levels in tissues

explanation: Spot on! When body tissues are short on oxygen over time, the body panics and pumps out more red blood cells to help.

question: What is the classic symptom reported by a patient with a rectovaginal fistula?

options.A: Inability to empty the bladder completely
options.B: Severe sharp pain during ovulation
options.C: Passage of gas or stool through the vagina
options.D: Continuous watery discharge from the urethra

explanation: Because of the abnormal opening, bowel contents escape through the vaginal canal instead of the anus. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T13#GNS216_U5_T13_h4)

question: Which medication is a core part of the preferred first-line ART treatment for adults in Nigeria?

options.A: Paracetamol
options.B: Dolutegravir
options.C: Insulin
options.D: Penicillin

explanation: Correct! Dolutegravir is a powerful, safe integrase inhibitor that forms the backbone of standard first-line HIV treatment in Nigeria today.

question: Why do we recommend putting petroleum jelly on a healing biopsy site instead of letting a hard crust form?

options.A: Ointment prevents the local anesthetic from wearing off too early
options.B: Petroleum jelly contains strong antibiotics to kill all skin bacteria
options.C: It prevents the sutures from dissolving before the skin closes
options.D: A moist environment helps new skin cells migrate and heal faster

explanation: Skin cells love moisture! Keeping the wound soft with ointment lets new skin cells slide across and close the gap much faster than when a dry, crunchy scab is in the way.

question: When should a patient with chronic pancreatitis take their prescribed pancreatic enzyme replacement therapy?

options.A: With every meal and snack
options.B: Only when eating foods high in sugar
options.C: Only when abdominal pain begins
options.D: Once daily right before bedtime

explanation: Spot on! Enzymes need to be taken right along with all food and snacks so they can mix with the nutrients and help the body digest food properly.

question: What is the main goal of a Drug Revolving Fund (DRF) in a public hospital?

options.A: To fund free medical care for all citizens indefinitely
options.B: To generate large commercial profits for hospital expansion
options.C: To replace the national health ministry budget entirely
options.D: To guarantee a steady, continuous supply of essential medicines

explanation: Spot on! The whole point of a DRF is to make sure the pharmacy never runs out of crucial drugs by using a self-replenishing pool of money.

question: What is a major benefit of community genetic counseling for inherited blood disorders?

options.A: Manufacturing safe blood products for local hospital use
options.B: Providing free meals for patients with severe chronic anemia
options.C: Helping families understand their risk of passing conditions to children
options.D: Treating acute bleeding episodes in emergency rooms

explanation: Genetic counseling educates couples about their carrier status and the statistical chances of having children with conditions like sickle cell anemia. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T15#GNS311_U2_T15_h7)

question: Which chemical agent requires a special airing-out (aeration) period because it leaves toxic gas behind?

options.A: Ordinary liquid soap
options.B: Hydrogen peroxide
options.C: Ethylene oxide
options.D: Standard tap water

explanation: Ethylene oxide is a strong sterilizing gas, but items need to sit in a special aeration chamber afterward to clear out lingering toxic fumes.

question: What is always the very first step in a basic reflex arc?

options.A: Effector muscle
options.B: Motor neuron
options.C: Sensory receptor
options.D: Integration center

explanation: Every reflex starts with detection! A sensory receptor has to first notice the stimulus—like a sudden stretch, heat, or pain—before anything else can happen.

question: Why is encapsulation often used specifically for pharmaceutical waste?

options.A: To turn expired tablets into sweet-tasting liquid syrups
options.B: To immobilize chemical drugs and prevent them from entering water supplies
options.C: To bleach colored medicine bottles so they can be recycled
options.D: To make heavy metal containers easier to burn in an incinerator

explanation: Encapsulation binds drugs in a solid matrix like cement, stopping them from dissolving and leaching into soil and groundwater. [learn more](GNS122_U3_T15#GNS122_U3_T15_h5)

question: What is the primary physical cause of obstetric fistula in young mothers?

options.A: Severe malnutrition during early childhood
options.B: A hereditary genetic blood disorder
options.C: Exposure to industrial chemical toxins
options.D: Prolonged and obstructed labor without timely surgical care

explanation: Obstetric fistula happens when labor gets stuck for too long without medical help. The constant pressure creates a tear or opening between the birth canal and the bladder or rectum. Timely medical care prevents this tragic injury.

question: Why is 'Risk for Infection' a top concern when a patient's white blood cell count is low?

options.A: The patient is forced to share a room with other sick individuals
options.B: The body lacks sufficient defense mechanisms to fight off invading pathogens
options.C: Intravenous lines always cause immediate blood infections
options.D: Hospital linens usually harbor resistant bacterial strains

explanation: White blood cells are our frontline soldiers against germs. When numbers are down, even friendly germs can become a big problem. Protection is key!

question: What is the main goal of placing the harvested skin sample into normal saline or water?

options.A: To sterilize the sample from any surface bacterial contamination
options.B: To encourage the microfilariae to emerge out into the fluid
options.C: To dissolve the tissue completely so only DNA remains
options.D: To preserve the tissue for permanent paraffin embedding

explanation: Spot on! The liquid tricks the live microfilariae into crawling right out of the skin snippet so we can spot them under the microscope.

question: What is the main goal of medications used for degenerative neurological disorders?

options.A: To replace damaged neurons with new tissue
options.B: To relieve symptoms and improve quality of life
options.C: To speed up the cellular breakdown process
options.D: To completely cure the underlying disease

explanation: Right now, medicines can't cure these diseases or stop nerve loss, but they do a great job easing symptoms so patients stay comfortable. Keep up the awesome studying!

question: Which of these everyday ward items belongs to the general waste category?

options.A: Food wrappers from the ward kitchen
options.B: Used hypodermic needles
options.C: Surgically removed tissue samples
options.D: Expired antibiotic tablets

explanation: That's correct! General waste is non-hazardous and similar to ordinary household rubbish, like paper and food packaging.

question: Which body landmark separates upper GI bleeding from lower GI bleeding?

options.A: Anorectal line
options.B: Pyloric sphincter
options.C: Ileocecal valve
options.D: Ligament of Treitz

explanation: The ligament of Treitz sits right where the duodenum meets the jejunum, serving as the official dividing line for GI bleeding.

question: What should you do right away if you evaluate your patient and see they haven't met their care goal?

options.A: Wait until the next morning doctor's rounds to report it
options.B: Discontinue all monitoring devices to reduce patient stress
options.C: Reassess the patient and modify the plan of care
options.D: Document that the patient is impossible to treat

explanation: Don't panic if a goal isn't met—that's totally normal nursing! It just means it's time to cycle back, figure out what's going on, and tweak your game plan.

question: Which of these is a typical feature of a benign (non-cancerous) tumor?

options.A: Surrounded by a fibrous capsule
options.B: Infiltrates surrounding normal tissues
options.C: Rapid and uncontrolled cellular division
options.D: Ability to form secondary tumors

explanation: Correct! Benign tumors usually stay put inside a neat fibrous capsule, meaning they don't invade nearby tissues or spread around.

question: What is a major requirement for medical equipment used inside an aircraft?

options.A: It must be lightweight and battery-operated
options.B: It must be made entirely of glass and porcelain
options.C: It must be larger than standard hospital monitors
options.D: It must plug directly into standard wall sockets

explanation: Brilliant! Space and power are limited in aircraft, so all gear has to be portable, light, and run smoothly on reliable batteries.

question: Which feature is unique to Crohn's disease when compared to ulcerative colitis?

options.A: It is caused directly by a specific bacterial infection
options.B: Damage is strictly limited to the inner lining of the colon
options.C: It features patchy 'skip lesions' and inflammation through all layers of the bowel wall
options.D: Inflammation is continuous and always starts from the rectum

explanation: Crohn's can affect the entire thickness of the bowel wall (transmural) and likes to leave healthy patches of tissue right next to diseased ones (skip lesions).

question: While trying to do a manual flush, you feel a lot of resistance on the syringe plunger. What is your next move?

options.A: Push harder on the plunger to force the clot out
options.B: Inject twice as much fluid to clear the blockage
options.C: Pull the catheter halfway out of the urethra
options.D: Stop pushing immediately and report the resistance

explanation: Never force it! Pushing against a blockage can tear the delicate bladder wall or urethra. Stop and let the doctor know.

question: What does a black, tarry stool sample usually tell you about your patient?

options.A: Bleeding in the upper gastrointestinal tract
options.B: Bleeding in the lower rectum or anus
options.C: Severe dehydration and low fluid intake
options.D: A high intake of green leafy vegetables

explanation: As blood travels all the way from the stomach through the gut, digestive juices break it down, turning it dark and tarry by the time it comes out.

question: What type of acid-base imbalance builds up in the body during prolonged oxygen shortage?

options.A: Metabolic alkalosis
options.B: Respiratory acidosis
options.C: Metabolic acidosis
options.D: Respiratory alkalosis

explanation: Since anaerobic metabolism produces lactic acid, that acid buildup leads straight to metabolic acidosis. Great clinical connection to keep in mind!

question: What two things happen to blood gases at the exact same time during asphyxia?

options.A: High oxygen and low carbon dioxide
options.B: Low oxygen and high carbon dioxide
options.C: High oxygen and high carbon dioxide
options.D: Low oxygen and low carbon dioxide

explanation: Think of asphyxia as a double trouble situation: oxygen drops (hypoxia) while carbon dioxide gets trapped inside the body (hypercapnia). You've got this!

question: What do we mean by the term 'gender roles'?

options.A: The legal medical definitions used in hospitals
options.B: The specific genetic markers found on human chromosomes
options.C: Societal expectations and behaviors considered appropriate for men and women
options.D: The biological hormones produced by the endocrine glands

explanation: Correct! Gender roles are the cultural rules and tasks society assigns based on perceived gender.

question: What is the danger of giving a central cough suppressant to a patient who has a chest full of thick mucus?

options.A: The mucus instantly dissolves into clear water.
options.B: Blood pressure drops to dangerous levels.
options.C: Mucus can accumulate and block the airways.
options.D: The patient begins breathing twice as fast.

explanation: If a patient has productive phlegm, they need to cough it out! Suppressing that reflex traps the gunk inside and can lead to worse blockages.

question: Why must sterile fields and items always be kept above waist level?

options.A: Hospital policies dictate that lower shelves are for waste
options.B: Gravity pulls heavier dust particles upward toward the chest
options.C: It prevents back strain during prolonged surgical procedures
options.D: Items below the waist are out of the nurse's direct line of sight

explanation: Anything below the waist or out of vision cannot be reliably monitored for contamination, so it is treated as unsterile. [learn more](GNS311_U4_T1#GNS311_U4_T1_h3)

question: Why is a urinalysis always done when checking for stress incontinence?

options.A: To check kidney function and filtration rates
options.B: To measure the exact amount of residual urine left in the bladder
options.C: To test the patient for diabetes and high blood sugar levels
options.D: To rule out a urinary tract infection that can cause similar symptoms

explanation: Infections can mimic incontinence by irritating the bladder, so checking the urine first helps doctors make a clear diagnosis.

question: What is a great, simple first step a nurse can suggest to an overweight teenager looking to improve their diet?

options.A: Replace sugary sodas and packaged drinks with water.
options.B: Consume only liquid protein shakes until target weight is met.
options.C: Eliminate all carbohydrates from daily meals completely.
options.D: Fast for two full days every week to jumpstart weight loss.

explanation: Spot on! Swapping out sugary drinks for water cuts down on empty liquid calories easily without driving the teen toward unhealthy crash diets.

question: What is the term for white blood cells squeezing through tiny blood vessel walls into injured tissue?

options.A: Vasoconstriction
options.B: Hemostasis
options.C: Apoptosis
options.D: Diapedesis

explanation: Great job! Diapedesis is just the clever way white blood cells slip out of the bloodstream to join the fight at the tissue level.

question: Which vital sign change usually comes with a widespread inflammatory response?

options.A: Elevated blood oxygen
options.B: Decreased heart rate
options.C: Elevated temperature
options.D: Lowered respiratory rate

explanation: Correct! Fever is a classic full-body response triggered when inflammatory signals talk to the brain's temperature control center.

question: What is often the very first sign that a patient is bleeding after having their tonsils out?

options.A: Frequent swallowing
options.B: Sudden abdominal cramping
options.C: A drop in body temperature
options.D: Complaints of severe foot pain

explanation: Spot on! Since blood pools quietly in the back of the throat after surgery, swallowing a lot is usually your early clue before any throwing up happens.

question: Why does HIV rely on the enzyme reverse transcriptase once it enters a host cell?

options.A: To cut open the host cell membrane
options.B: To repair damaged viral genetic material
options.C: To destroy competing white blood cells
options.D: To convert viral RNA into DNA

explanation: Think of reverse transcriptase as a translator. It changes the virus's RNA into DNA so the instructions can blend right into the host cell's own chromosomes!

question: Why is a complete large bowel blockage considered a serious medical emergency?

options.A: High pressure can cause the bowel wall to rupture and spill contents
options.B: It immediately stops the kidneys from producing urine
options.C: It stops the liver from filtering toxins from the blood
options.D: It always causes permanent brain damage within two hours

explanation: Spot on! As gas and stool pile up behind the blockage, pressure builds, cutting off blood flow and risking a dangerous rupture (perforation).

question: What is the correct sequence when putting on personal protective equipment before entering an isolation room?

options.A: Eye protection, gloves, gown, mask
options.B: Gloves, gown, mask, eye protection
options.C: Gown, mask, eye protection, gloves
options.D: Mask, gloves, gown, eye protection

explanation: Putting the gown on first and gloves last ensures the glove cuffs overlap the gown sleeves, leaving no exposed skin at the wrist. [learn more](GNS123_U4_T4#GNS123_U4_T4_h6)

question: What is the main goal of musculoskeletal rehabilitation?

options.A: To accelerate the natural clotting of fractured bones
options.B: To completely eliminate all chronic joint inflammation
options.C: To restore functional capacity and independence
options.D: To replace lost surgical muscle mass with scar tissue

explanation: Great job! Rehab is all about helping patients get back on their feet so they can do their daily activities and live independently.

question: Why do doctors order diagnostic tests in reproductive health?

options.A: To permanently cure all chronic reproductive tract infections
options.B: To replace the need for a physical clinical examination
options.C: To induce immediate menopause in older female patients
options.D: To investigate underlying structural or hormonal abnormalities

explanation: Spot on! Diagnostic tests help us figure out the root cause of any structural, hormonal, or functional issues in the reproductive system. You've got this!

question: What is the main goal of continuous bladder irrigation (CBI) after prostate surgery?

options.A: To deliver strong antibiotic drugs directly to the prostate tissue
options.B: To permanently shrink any remaining benign prostate cells
options.C: To measure the exact daily hormonal output of the testes
options.D: To prevent blood clot retention and keep the catheter open

explanation: After surgery, bleeding can form clots that block the catheter. CBI flushes fluid in and out continuously to keep everything clear and flowing!

question: What tells your kidneys to release erythropoietin (EPO) to make more red blood cells?

options.A: High blood pressure in the arteries
options.B: The presence of bacterial toxins
options.C: Low oxygen levels in the blood
options.D: An excess of circulating platelets

explanation: Correct! When your kidneys sense your body isn't getting quite enough oxygen, they send out EPO like an alarm bell to tell your bone marrow to pump out more red blood cells.

question: What is the main goal of using skull traction for someone with a neck injury?

options.A: To align and stabilize damaged cervical vertebrae
options.B: To completely replace the need for future spinal surgery
options.C: To deliver intravenous pain medication directly to the neck
options.D: To increase blood flow to the brain tissues

explanation: You've got this! Skull traction gently pulls to put broken or dislocated neck bones back into place and keeps them steady so they can heal safely.

question: Why should you avoid pouring harsh surgical scrubs directly inside an open wound?

options.A: It can damage exposed tissue cells and delay proper wound healing
options.B: It instantly inactivates any local anesthetic you inject later
options.C: It permanently stains the surrounding skin a bright yellow color
options.D: It causes the skin edges to swell up and prevent knot tying

explanation: Harsh chemicals are too strong for delicate exposed cells inside a wound. Stick to normal saline for cleaning—your patients will heal much better!

question: What is the main difference between an inflammatory joint disease and osteoarthritis?

options.A: Localized bone fractures
options.B: Mechanical joint instability
options.C: Age-related cartilage wear
options.D: Immune-mediated synovitis

explanation: Think of inflammatory joint diseases as the immune system mistakenly attacking the joint lining (synovitis), while osteoarthritis is simply the wear and tear of cartilage as we age. Spotting this difference helps you understand why they are treated differently!

question: A client complains of heavy, painful periods and wants an IUD. Which type should you recommend to help with the heavy bleeding?

options.A: A hormonal IUD that releases levonorgestrel
options.B: A standard copper-bearing T 380A device
options.C: Any IUD, because all types stop bleeding completely
options.D: A plain plastic loop with no hormones or metal

explanation: Hormonal IUDs are great because they lighten the uterine lining over time, which usually means much lighter, less painful periods for the client.

question: How does a nurse act as an effective patient advocate regarding diagnostic imaging?

options.A: By insisting that every patient with joint pain gets a daily CT scan.
options.B: By deciding which diagnostic test a patient needs without consulting a doctor.
options.C: By telling patients that CT scans carry zero health risks of any kind.
options.D: By questioning unneeded scans and confirming that radiation safety steps are followed.

explanation: Nurses advocate for patients by verifying clinical justification, preventing unnecessary radiation exposure, and supporting safe imaging practices. [learn more](GNS222_U1_T6#GNS222_U1_T6_h6)

question: Up to how many days after childbirth can a mother's death still be classified as maternal mortality?

options.A: Ninety days
options.B: Forty-two days
options.C: Seven days
options.D: Fourteen days

explanation: You've got this! Officially, maternal death includes any death during pregnancy or within 42 days (6 weeks) after delivery. Keep that timeline in mind!

question: Why does taking strong, broad-spectrum antibiotics often lead to an annoying yeast infection?

options.A: It kills protective lactobacilli bacteria
options.B: It increases the production of vaginal glycogen
options.C: It lowers overall body temperature
options.D: It directly stimulates fungal spore production

explanation: Antibiotics are great, but they aren't picky—they wipe out our protective friendly bacteria right along with the bad ones, leaving yeast free to party! [learn more](GNS216_U5_T10#GNS216_U5_T10_h3)

question: Which of the following is linked as an environmental trigger for developing MS?

options.A: Living close to sea level in tropical zones
options.B: Engaging in heavy physical labor outdoors
options.C: Eating a diet high in processed carbohydrates
options.D: Past viral infections like Epstein-Barr virus

explanation: While the exact cause isn't fully pinned down, certain past viral infections are believed to help trigger this abnormal immune response in vulnerable people.

question: Why do doctors and nurses prefer feeding patients through the gut (enteral nutrition) rather than through a drip (parenteral nutrition) when possible?

options.A: It requires no special monitoring of blood glucose or laboratory tests
options.B: It helps maintain gut health and prevents bacteria from escaping into the body
options.C: It completely eliminates the risk of aspiration or gastrointestinal upset
options.D: It is absorbed directly into the bloodstream without needing digestion

explanation: Using the natural digestive tract keeps the gut lining strong and stops bad bacteria from wandering where they shouldn't!

question: A patient says they want to save half their leftover antibiotics for a family member who might fall sick later. How should you respond?

options.A: Explain the dangers of sharing medications and encourage proper disposal
options.B: Write down instructions on which family member should take the leftover pills
options.C: Advise the patient to double the dose next time someone coughs
options.D: Praise the patient for being resourceful and saving money

explanation: Wonderful! As a nurse, you want to warmly educate patients on why sharing drugs spreads resistance and toxicity.

question: As a nurse, what is your very first priority when a patient arrives with post-abortion complications?

options.A: Conducting a detailed interview about contraception history
options.B: Reporting the incident immediately to law enforcement
options.C: Asking about her religious and cultural beliefs
options.D: Evaluating airway, breathing, and circulation

explanation: Safety first! Emergency nursing always starts with the ABCs to stabilize vital signs and catch shock or heavy bleeding early.

question: Why shouldn't a nurse just do everything for a slow patient who can manage with a tool?

options.A: To save nursing time for charting and other patients
options.B: To ensure the patient finishes dressing before visiting hours
options.C: To foster independence and prevent learned helplessness
options.D: Because hospital policy strictly forbids nurse assistance

explanation: Brilliant! We want to cheer them on to do it themselves so they don't become overly dependent on us.

question: Which embryonic structures develop into the fallopian tubes?

options.A: Wolffian ducts
options.B: Gonadal ridges
options.C: Urogenital sinus
options.D: Müllerian ducts

explanation: Brilliant! The Müllerian ducts are the building blocks in the embryo that grow to form the fallopian tubes, uterus, and upper vagina.

question: What is the most appropriate initial response when a family member expresses anger toward the nursing staff?

options.A: Threaten to call security if they do not quiet down
options.B: Remain calm and acknowledge the emotional pain behind the anger
options.C: Argue back to prove that the hospital staff followed all rules
options.D: Walk out of the room immediately and refuse to return

explanation: Anger in healthcare is often a mask for fear and grief; acknowledging the underlying emotion helps de-escalate tension. [learn more](GNS321_U4_T6#GNS321_U4_T6_h6)

question: What is the primary goal of the living will movement?

options.A: To give doctors full authority over end-of-life care
options.B: To speed up the legal probate process for families
options.C: To help patients control their medical treatment choices ahead of time
options.D: To reduce overall hospital costs for elderly patients

explanation: The entire movement centers on letting individuals make their treatment preferences known before they lose the ability to speak for themselves. [learn more](GNS221_U4_T7#GNS221_U4_T7_h1)

question: What is the main danger when a nurse transcribes (copies) a medication order?

options.A: It removes the need for nurses to check patient identity
options.B: It makes doctors write prescriptions much slower than usual
options.C: It permanently deletes previous medication history from the chart
options.D: It introduces opportunities for human error and misinterpretation

explanation: Spot on! Every time an order is manually copied over, there's a risk that numbers, decimals, or abbreviations might be misread.

question: A patient on a hot day has been standing for hours at a parade and suddenly feels weak and collapses. What is the most likely trigger?

options.A: Peripheral blood pooling from heat and standing
options.B: A sudden increase in intracranial brain pressure
options.C: An acute blockage in the coronary arteries
options.D: An unrecognized epileptic seizure disorder

explanation: Heat and prolonged standing cause blood to pool in the legs, reducing return to the heart and triggering vasovagal fainting. [learn more](GNS123_U3_T16#GNS123_U3_T16_h3)

question: Why must you perform hand hygiene immediately after taking off your gloves?

options.A: Hospital policy requires washing hands twice per hour
options.B: Gloves make your hands smell unpleasant
options.C: Microorganisms may have transferred to your skin during removal
options.D: It helps the skin dry out after sweating inside rubber

explanation: Even with careful removal, tiny tears or contact with the outside of gloves can transfer germs to your hands. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T16#GNS122_U2_T16_h5)

question: Which parts of the body are involved in a lower respiratory tract infection?

options.A: Sinuses, tonsils, and Eustachian tubes
options.B: Nose, pharynx, and larynx
options.C: Oral cavity and epiglottis
options.D: Trachea, bronchi, and alveoli

explanation: Think of the larynx as the dividing line! Anything below it—like the windpipe (trachea), breathing tubes (bronchi), and air sacs (alveoli)—makes up the lower respiratory tract.

question: What are the two main systems combined within the genito-urinary tract?

options.A: The nervous and skeletal systems
options.B: The digestive and endocrine systems
options.C: The respiratory and circulatory systems
options.D: The urinary and reproductive systems

explanation: The genito-urinary system is a combination of the urinary tract organs and the reproductive organs due to their close developmental and physical links. [learn more](GNS213_U4_T1#GNS213_U4_T1_h1)

question: A pregnant teenager attends an antenatal clinic and exhibits signs she is at risk of being forced into early marriage. What is the most appropriate initial nursing action?

options.A: Ignore the situation because family matters are private
options.B: Call local police immediately while she is still in the exam room
options.C: Lecture her parents harshly in front of the other waiting patients
options.D: Provide a safe, confidential space to assess her safety and offer support

explanation: Creating a confidential environment allows the nurse to gauge immediate danger and connect the patient with protective services safely. [learn more](GNS312_U1_T18#GNS312_U1_T18_h6)

question: If a patient's lab report shows a dangerously abnormal potassium level, which body system is at the highest immediate risk?

options.A: Respiratory system
options.B: Digestive system
options.C: Cardiovascular system
options.D: Integumentary system

explanation: That's right! Potassium directly controls the electrical rhythm of muscle cells, which means the heart is at immediate risk if these levels go wild.

question: Why is it important to know if a seizure was 'provoked' by a temporary issue rather than epilepsy?

options.A: Epilepsy is strictly a pediatric condition that resolves after puberty
options.B: Provoked seizures never involve loss of consciousness
options.C: Provoked seizures are caused by temporary triggers and may not need lifelong drugs
options.D: Epilepsy can only be diagnosed if the patient has had at least ten seizures

explanation: Spot on! If a seizure is caused by something fixable like low sodium or a high fever, treating the root cause stops the seizures without needing long-term medication.

question: What is the main role of the family when supporting someone with a long-term condition like HIV?

options.A: Taking over all medical prescription duties
options.B: Isolating the patient from community stressors
options.C: Replacing the clinical healthcare team entirely
options.D: Acting as vital partners in the care continuum

explanation: You've got this! Families don't replace doctors or nurses; instead, they walk right beside the healthcare team to support the patient's long-term health journey.

question: What does "process monitoring" evaluate during a community health campaign?

options.A: The exact financial profit generated by local primary health clinics
options.B: Long-term genetic changes in the community's disease risk profile
options.C: The total number of hospital beds required for severe stroke patients
options.D: Day-to-day activities like attendance numbers and media broadcasts

explanation: Correct! Process monitoring is just checking your daily checklist: Are the workshops running? Are people showing up? Did the radio jingle play?

question: Why is careful documentation and evidence preservation important when treating a suspected assault?

options.A: It assists legal investigations and protects the patient's rights
options.B: It is required primarily to determine hospital insurance payouts
options.C: It speeds up the bone healing process following orthopedic trauma
options.D: It prevents the patient from experiencing psychological shock

explanation: Well done! Accurate medical notes and evidence preservation are crucial for legal investigations when dealing with intentional injuries.

question: What is the best initial nursing action if a patient has a painful ingrown toenail that looks a bit red?

options.A: Soak the foot in warm water and report it to the provider
options.B: Dig out the ingrown corner immediately using sterile forceps
options.C: Cut a deep V into the center of the nail to relieve pressure
options.D: Apply tight adhesive tape to pull the skin away from the nail

explanation: Correct! Warm soaks bring relief, but never try to dig out an ingrown nail yourself—always report it so it can be managed safely.

question: Which of these hospital items is considered critical and needs full sterilization?

options.A: A surgical scalpel blade
options.B: A reusable blood pressure cuff
options.C: A stethoscope chest piece
options.D: A bedside plastic commode

explanation: Brilliant! Scalpels cut deep into sterile body tissues, so they must be 100% free of all germs and spores through proper sterilization.

question: As a nurse, why should you avoid telling a panicked patient that 'everything will be fine'?

options.A: It violates standard hospital communication policy
options.B: It offers false reassurance that cannot be guaranteed
options.C: It forces the patient to become overly talkative
options.D: It increases the patient's heart rate immediately

explanation: Well done! Since we can't predict the future, promising that 'everything will be fine' can break trust if things take a turn. Honest, gentle grounding is always safer.

question: Why should pregnant women AVOID taking stimulant laxatives unless prescribed by a doctor?

options.A: They stop the kidneys from making urine
options.B: They instantly cause permanent blindness
options.C: They turn breast milk completely green
options.D: They can stimulate the uterus and potentially trigger contractions

explanation: Correct! Stimulant laxatives irritate the bowel walls so strongly that they can sometimes trigger unwanted uterine contractions.

question: Aside from clinical health, what major factor shapes a person's family planning choices?

options.A: Global weather patterns
options.B: Hospital bed capacity
options.C: Socio-cultural dynamics
options.D: Local taxi fare rates

explanation: You nailed it! Family planning choices are deeply tied to cultural traditions, beliefs, and community values, not just pure medicine.

question: Why do health programs often fail if nurses ignore local cultural values?

options.A: Because government laws forbid treating people with different beliefs
options.B: Because the community feels disrespected and rejects outside interference
options.C: Because local leaders charge heavy fines for unapproved advice
options.D: Because medications lose their chemical potency in different cultures

explanation: Always respect local culture! When people feel understood and respected, they are much more likely to welcome healthcare programs.

question: What happens right away when a bone gets fractured?

options.A: Immediate hardening of a permanent bony callus
options.B: Rapid degradation of surrounding articular cartilage
options.C: Instant conversion of osteoblasts into osteoclasts
options.D: Formation of a blood clot or fracture hematoma

explanation: When a bone breaks, blood vessels tear, and blood pools around the area to form a protective clot (hematoma) to kick off healing.

question: What should healthy, normal cerebrospinal fluid look like?

options.A: Dark red and viscous
options.B: Clear and colorless
options.C: Milky and opaque
options.D: Yellow and thick

explanation: Correct! Normal cerebrospinal fluid looks just like clean, pure water.

question: When should reusable items like a blood pressure cuff be disinfected?

options.A: Between every individual patient use
options.B: Once at the end of each nursing shift
options.C: Only when visibly stained with blood
options.D: Once a week during deep cleaning

explanation: Spot on! To stop cross-contamination between patients, always clean and disinfect reusable equipment after every single use.

question: An elevated white blood cell (WBC) count usually points to what in a patient?

options.A: Severe dehydration
options.B: Iron deficiency anemia
options.C: Chronic kidney failure
options.D: Infection or inflammation

explanation: Great job! White blood cells are our body's soldiers. When they shoot up in number, it usually means they are busy fighting off an infection or inflammation.

question: While listening to a pregnant patient with a Doppler, you hear a rhythmic sound matching her pulse. What should you do?

options.A: Record this rate immediately as the baby's heart rate
options.B: Assume the fetus has severe bradycardia and prep for emergency
options.C: Recognize this is the maternal pulse and keep searching for the faster fetal heartbeat
options.D: Stop the assessment because the machine is broken

explanation: Great job! Maternal blood vessels run through the uterus, so you always want to double-check that you're counting the baby's heart rate, not mum's.

question: What must the nurse check or do immediately before pulling back the syringe plunger to create a vacuum?

options.A: Boil the entire plastic syringe in hot water
options.B: Attach a heavy electrical cord to the back handle
options.C: Ensure the vacuum valves or buttons are closed
options.D: Fill the cylinder completely with sterile water

explanation: If the valves are left open while pulling the plunger, air simply enters the syringe from the outside and no vacuum is created. [learn more](GNS226_U5_T010#GNS226_U5_T010_h3)

question: As a nurse, why shouldn't you focus only on the physical symptoms of a blood disorder?

options.A: Hospital management policies require psychological notes for discharge
options.B: Physical symptoms are rarely relevant to the patient's actual recovery
options.C: Emotional distress and physical pain deeply affect overall quality of life
options.D: Blood disorders only impact the emotional state of the patient

explanation: Spot on! Holistic nursing means remembering that a patient's mind and body are connected. Healing involves caring for both.

question: Why do nurses monitor hourly urine output so closely when caring for a patient in shock?

options.A: It prevents the urinary bladder from overstretching during fluid resuscitation
options.B: It confirms whether the patient has a urinary tract infection
options.C: It is a reliable indicator of renal perfusion and overall organ blood flow
options.D: It directly measures the current blood glucose levels in the bloodstream

explanation: Your kidneys are like little warning lights. If they aren't making urine, it tells you they aren't getting enough blood flow—which means other vital organs are likely suffering too.

question: Which bacterial STI is famous for causing a classic, usually painless sore called a chancre in its early stage?

options.A: Chlamydia
options.B: Candidiasis
options.C: Gonorrhoea
options.D: Syphilis

explanation: That's primary syphilis! It loves to throw patients off because the initial sore (chancre) doesn't hurt at all, so people often ignore it.

question: If an older male patient has an enlarged prostate (BPH), what urinary symptom is he most likely to complain about?

options.A: A weak and slow urinary stream
options.B: Total absence of urine production
options.C: Inability to control bowel movements
options.D: Severe pain during bladder filling

explanation: Makes total sense, right? When the prostate grows, it presses on the urethra like a pinched garden hose, making the urine flow slow and weak.

question: In a burn wound, what is the central area called where the maximum tissue damage happens?

options.A: Zone of hyperemia
options.B: Zone of inflammation
options.C: Zone of stasis
options.D: Zone of coagulation

explanation: Think of the zone of coagulation as ground zero—it's closest to the heat, so the cells are completely destroyed and can't recover. You've got this!

question: Why are children with acute osteomyelitis at risk for long-term bone growth issues?

options.A: Bones in children never fully heal once inflamed
options.B: Antibiotics used in pediatrics actively dissolve healthy cartilage
options.C: Children lack any ability to form new bone after an infection
options.D: The infection can damage nearby growth plates, altering future bone growth

explanation: Kids are still growing! If an infection spreads into their growth plates (epiphyseal plates), it can mess with how that bone grows as they get older.

question: Which heart rhythm is a life-threatening emergency that requires immediate CPR and defibrillation?

options.A: Atrial fibrillation
options.B: Premature atrial contractions
options.C: Ventricular fibrillation
options.D: Sinus bradycardia

explanation: Ventricular fibrillation (V-fib) is a true medical emergency! The lower chambers just quiver instead of pumping, meaning no blood flows. Quick CPR and a shock are literal lifesavers here.

question: Why do we measure blood pressure in millimeters of mercury (mmHg)?

options.A: It measures the exact weight of blood inside the heart
options.B: It estimates the total oxygen carried by red blood cells
options.C: It is the standard unit based on historical manometers
options.D: It calculates the chemical composition of plasma

explanation: It's all history! Early blood pressure tools (manometers) actually used columns of liquid mercury, and the mmHg unit stuck around to this day.

question: Which measurement is frequently referred to as the fifth vital sign?

options.A: Weight
options.B: Height
options.C: Urinary output
options.D: Pain

explanation: Pain is routinely assessed alongside traditional vital signs to monitor patient comfort and well-being. [learn more](GNS112_U6_T1#GNS112_U6_T1_h5)

question: What is the main difference between airborne and droplet transmission?

options.A: Droplet particles can travel for miles across different cities
options.B: Droplet transmission requires a mosquito bite to start working
options.C: Airborne droplet nuclei stay suspended in the air much longer
options.D: Airborne particles only spread through contaminated drinking water

explanation: Airborne transmission involves tiny particles that stay in the air and travel far, whereas large droplets quickly fall to the ground. [learn more](GNS123_U4_T5#GNS123_U4_T5_h4)

question: Which hormone, released when you are under long-term stress, tends to lower your immune response?

options.A: Thyroxine
options.B: Cortisol
options.C: Melatonin
options.D: Insulin

explanation: Well done! High cortisol from chronic stress acts like a brake on your immune system, which is why stressed students easily catch colds during exams!

question: Which lethal heart rhythm requires immediate defibrillation and emergency response?

options.A: First-degree heart block
options.B: Sinus bradycardia
options.C: Premature atrial contractions
options.D: Ventricular fibrillation

explanation: Ventricular fibrillation is a chaotic heart rhythm where the ventricles quiver instead of pumping blood, causing cardiac arrest that requires immediate electrical shock. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T13#GNS213_U1_T13_h4)

question: What is a big advantage of a PET scan over a standard CT scan in cancer care?

options.A: It highlights active areas to tell scar tissue apart from live tumor
options.B: It can be done instantly at the bedside without a machine
options.C: It measures the exact amount of haemoglobin in red cells
options.D: It uses no radiation and needs no dye

explanation: PET scans track cellular activity, helping doctors see if a leftover mass is still active cancer or just harmless scar tissue.

question: Which sign is a classic clue that someone has hyperthyroidism?

options.A: SlOWed heart rate and sluggish mentation
options.B: Intolerance to cold room temperatures
options.C: Severe constipation and dry coarse skin
options.D: Weight loss despite an increased appetite

explanation: Hyperthyroidism puts the body's engine into overdrive! Patients burn through calories so fast that they lose weight even though they are eating way more food than usual.

question: Why do patients often feel so exhausted and confused right after a major fit?

options.A: The seizure permanently destroyed parts of their memory
options.B: Their blood pressure dropped to dangerous levels
options.C: Their brain cells used up a lot of energy and need to recover
options.D: They received too much medication during the episode

explanation: Think of a seizure like a sudden electrical storm in the brain. It burns through so much energy that the brain needs some quiet time to recharge afterwards. Completely normal recovery!

question: Which tocolytic drug is usually avoided past 32 weeks because it can affect the baby's heart circulation?

options.A: Indomethacin
options.B: Magnesium sulfate
options.C: Terbutaline
options.D: Nifedipine

explanation: Indomethacin is a prostaglandin blocker, but we have to be careful using it late in pregnancy so it doesn't cause early closure of the baby's ductus arteriosus. Excellent pharmacological safety!

question: What is the typical safe suction pressure range for an adult patient?

options.A: 500 to 600 mmHg
options.B: 10 to 20 mmHg
options.C: 80 to 120 mmHg
options.D: 200 to 300 mmHg

explanation: Pressures between 80 and 120 mmHg are strong enough to remove thick mucus without causing excessive trauma to the airway lining. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T12#GNS212_U2_T12_h3)

question: How is a vasospasm different from atherosclerosis?

options.A: Vasospasm only affects veins, while atherosclerosis affects capillaries
options.B: Vasospasm is a temporary muscle squeeze, whereas plaque is a structural buildup
options.C: Vasospasm takes decades to form, whereas plaque forms in seconds
options.D: Vasospasm causes permanent damage, while plaque always goes away

explanation: A vasospasm is just a sudden, temporary twitch or squeeze of the muscle in the blood vessel wall. Atherosclerosis, on the other hand, is a long-term buildup of fatty gunk.

question: Which vitamin is synthesized in the skin when exposed to sunlight?

options.A: Vitamin C
options.B: Vitamin D
options.C: Vitamin K
options.D: Vitamin A

explanation: Ultraviolet light helps convert cholesterol compounds in the skin into active vitamin D precursors necessary for bone health. [learn more](GNS211_U2_T1#GNS211_U2_T1_h6)

question: Which physical sign tells you that a patient's peripheral tissues are poorly perfused?

options.A: Rapid pupillary reaction
options.B: Bounding carotid pulses
options.C: Cool and mottled extremities
options.D: Warm and flushed skin tone

explanation: When blood flow drops, the body saves blood for vital organs, leaving the hands and feet cold and blotchy.

question: Which specific immune cells does HIV attack and destroy?

options.A: Red blood cells
options.B: Platelets
options.C: Neutrophils
options.D: CD4+ T helper cells

explanation: HIV targets CD4+ T helper cells, weakening the body's immune defenses over time. You've got this!

question: A stroke patient is struggling to hold a spoon because of weak arms. What should you do?

options.A: Initiate assisted feeding to ensure the patient gets enough food
options.B: Insist the patient feed themselves to encourage independence
options.C: Withhold meals until the patient regains full arm strength
options.D: Switch the patient immediately to total parenteral nutrition

explanation: Great clinical instinct! When weakness gets in the way of holding utensils safely, stepping in with assisted feeding keeps your patient nourished and cared for.

question: What is the name of the smooth inner lining of a joint capsule that gets inflamed in many rheumatic disorders?

options.A: Endosteum
options.B: Synovium
options.C: Periosteum
options.D: Myocardium

explanation: The synovium is the delicate membrane lining our joints. When inflammatory conditions flare up, this lining is usually the main target of the immune response.

question: What is the biggest downside to using benzodiazepines over a long period?

options.A: They carry a high risk of tolerance and physical dependence.
options.B: They cause severe weight loss in all patients.
options.C: They permanently destroy brain neurotransmitters.
options.D: They take at least six weeks to start working.

explanation: Benzodiazepines work fast, which is great for quick relief. But the body gets used to them quickly, leading to addiction and dependency if used long-term.

question: How do normal proto-oncogenes cause trouble when they mutate?

options.A: They permanently shut down all cellular activity in the organ
options.B: They cause the immune system to destroy healthy tissue
options.C: They stop the tumor from getting a blood supply
options.D: They become overactive oncogenes that drive constant cell division

explanation: Spot on! When proto-oncogenes mutate, they turn into hyperactive oncogenes that act like a stuck accelerator pedal, shouting for the cell to multiply nonstop.

question: What causes a follicular ovarian cyst to form?

options.A: The corpus luteum seals over and traps fluid inside
options.B: A benign tumor grows from surface epithelial cells
options.C: Endometrial cells attach to the outer surface of the ovary
options.D: A follicle fails to rupture and release an egg

explanation: Sometimes a fluid-filled egg sac just forgets to pop open and release its egg during ovulation. Instead, it keeps growing larger as a simple cyst!

question: A patient with a broken hip is placed in skin traction mainly for which reason?

options.A: Preventing deep vein thrombosis in the affected leg
options.B: Immediate rehabilitation and walking exercise practice
options.C: Permanent alignment so surgical repair is no longer required
options.D: Temporary stabilization and comfort while waiting for surgery

explanation: Think of skin traction here as a helpful temporary pause—it keeps the leg steady and comfortable until the surgical team is ready. You're doing great!

question: What is the main difference between a delayed union and a nonunion?

options.A: Delayed union requires surgery, while nonunion heals on its own with rest.
options.B: Delayed union takes longer than normal, while nonunion fails to heal entirely.
options.C: Delayed union involves infection, while nonunion is caused by blood clots.
options.D: Delayed union happens in children, while nonunion happens only in the elderly.

explanation: Think of delayed union as a slow student who eventually finishes the exam, while nonunion means the student simply gave up and stopped trying altogether.

question: Why do people with the same genetic background sometimes have different cancer risks?

options.A: Genetics is the only factor that ever influences disease
options.B: Inherited genes change completely every five years
options.C: Their environmental exposures and lifestyle choices vary
options.D: Lifestyle habits have no real impact on cellular health

explanation: Environmental and lifestyle factors interact with genes, meaning different habits will alter overall risk even among family members. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T1#GNS321_U1_T1_h5)

question: In very poor communities, what is one of the most common reasons families push young daughters into early marriage?

options.A: Mandatory taxes imposed on unmarried youth
options.B: Government incentives for young families
options.C: The high cost of hosting large wedding events
options.D: The desire to reduce household financial burdens

explanation: You've got it! Extreme poverty forces some struggling families to marry off young daughters simply to have one less mouth to feed.

question: How does an open fracture differ from a closed fracture?

options.A: Open fractures have a skin wound communicating with the break
options.B: Closed fractures involve multiple pieces of shattered bone
options.C: Closed fractures always require immediate surgical metal plating
options.D: Open fractures only occur in elderly patients with weak bones

explanation: The defining feature of an open fracture is a break in the skin that exposes the bone directly to the outside air. [learn more](GNS221_U3_T13#GNS221_U3_T13_h1)

question: How can community cultural norms impact how people seek medical care?

question: Which of these is NOT a typical challenge faced in everyday rehabilitation nursing?
